chunks: Ali ibn Abdullah al-Warraq narrated to me, saying: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated from al-Haytham ibn Abi al-Masruq al-Nahdi from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl

He said: I stayed in Batn Murr and was afflicted by the 'Madini vein' in my side and in my leg. I entered upon Ar-Rida (peace be upon him) in Medina, and he (peace be upon him) said: 'Why do I see you in pain?' I said: 'When I arrived at Batn Murr, the Madini vein afflicted me in my side and in my leg.' He (peace be upon him) pointed to what was in my side under the armpit, spoke some words, and spat upon it, then said (peace be upon him): 'There is no harm upon you from this.' He looked at what was in my leg and said: 'Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: Whoever of our Shias is afflicted with a calamity and remains patient, Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, will record for him the reward of a thousand martyrs.' I said to myself: 'By God, I will not be cured of my leg forever.' Al-Haytham said: 'So he continued limping from it until he died.'

key_terms.أَلْفِ شَهِيدٍ: A thousand martyrs, referring to the spiritual reward recorded by Allah for patient sufferers.
key_terms.الْعِرْقُ الْمَدِينِيُّ: A specific ailment or pain referred to as the 'Madini vein', affecting the side and leg.
key_terms.بَطْنُ مَرٍّ: A place name, Batn Murr, located on the route to Mecca.
key_terms.تَحْتَ الْإِبْطِ: Under the armpit, indicating the specific location of the ailment in the side.
key_terms.يَعْرُجُ: He limped or walked with a limp, describing the narrator's condition after the event.

ai.seo_question: What is the reward for patience in calamity according to Imam Ar-Rida (peace be upon him)?
ai.summary: This narration from *Uyun Akhbar al-Rida* highlights the dual nature of Imam al-Rida’s (a.s.) authority, demonstrating both his power to heal specific ailments like 'Al-Irq al-Madini' and his role as a teacher of spiritual endurance. By citing the tradition of Abu Ja'far (Imam al-Baqir) regarding the reward of a thousand martyrs for patience, the Imam contextualizes physical suffering within the broader Shia framework of *sabr* (patience) and divine recompense. The enduring limp serves as a tangible sign (*ayat*) of his leadership, illustrating that while healing is possible, the spiritual merit of enduring the trial remains paramount.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 47-39 Ali ibn Abdullah al-Warraq - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Sa’d ibn Abdullah quoted on the authority of al-Haytham ibn Abil Masrooq an-Nahdi, on the authority of Muhammad ibn al-Fuzayl,

“When we got to a place called Batn Murr being located one way-station before Mecca. I got side and leg pains called ‘Al-Irq al-Madini’ in Arabic. I went to see Ar-Ridha’ (a.s.) in Medina and he (a.s.) asked, ‘What is the cause of your pain?’ I said, ‘I got ‘Al-Irq pains in my legs and side when I reached Batn Murr. Ar-Ridha’ (a.s.) then pointed at what was on my side, said a few words and put some of his saliva on it and said, ‘You will no longer suffer from any side pains.’ Ar-Ridha’ (a.s.) then looked at my legs and said, ‘O Abu Ja’far! The Honorable the Exalted God will record the rewards of a thousand martyrs for whomever of our followers who suffers from a calamity and perseveres.’ I told myself, ‘By God, I will not be relieved of this pain in my legs until I die.’ The narrator added, “He limped for the rest of his life.”
